lesson.title: The Minus Sign That Flips the World: The Inverting Input
lesson.summary: The inverting input, marked with a minus sign on the op-amp symbol, is the terminal where a rising voltage drives the op-amp's output down, a direct consequence of the huge open-loop gain built into every operational amplifier.
lesson.body:
The op-amp symbol's triangle has two input leads on its flat left side, one marked with a minus sign and one with a plus sign. This chapter looks closely at the minus lead, the inverting input, and what that label actually means for the signal applied there.

An ideal operational amplifier, before any external feedback wiring is added, obeys a very simple rule: it takes the voltage difference between its two inputs and multiplies that difference by an enormous open-loop gain, Vout = Aol * (V+ - V-), where Aol is typically in the tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands for a real device. Look closely at that formula and the name inverting input makes itself obvious: if V+ is held fixed and V- rises, the quantity (V+ - V-) becomes more negative, and since Aol is a large positive number, Vout swings negative. Push voltage up at the inverting input, and the output moves down. That behavior is baked into the op-amp's internal differential amplifier structure; it happens whether or not any feedback network is connected.

Here is a worked example that shows just how dramatic this effect is. Suppose an op-amp has an open-loop gain of Aol = 100,000, a realistic value for many real devices, with V+ held at 0 V and V- raised to just 50 microvolts above that, 0.00005 V. The ideal output is Vout = 100,000 x (0 - 0.00005) = 100,000 x (-0.00005) = -5 V. A voltage difference smaller than a tenth of a millivolt, smaller than most people could even measure with a basic multimeter, produced a full 5 volt swing at the output, and it swung negative because the disturbance was applied to the inverting input.

That sensitivity is exactly why an op-amp is almost never used open-loop for linear signal processing: with a gain of 100,000, it would take only about 150 microvolts of input difference to drive a typical +/-15 V supply output all the way to one rail, and any tiny offset or noise voltage would do exactly that. The inverting input's real power only becomes usable once a feedback path is added back from the output to this same terminal, which is the subject of the negative feedback chapter later in this section. For now, the essential fact to hold onto is the sign: whatever voltage is applied directly to the inverting input, relative to the non-inverting input, the output moves in the opposite direction, scaled by the op-amp's very large open-loop gain.
